t: Minimum Operations to Make a Subsequence — Turning LCS into LIS
o: Only insertions are allowed, and afterwards target must appear as a subsequence of arr. The accounting is clean: whatever longest common subsequence (LCS) of target and arr already exists can be kept as-is, and every remaining target element needs exactly one insertion, so the answer is len(target) − LCS(target, arr). Example 1: target = [5,1,3], arr = [9,4,2,3,4]; their LCS is just [3], hence 3 − 1 = 2 insertions, e.g. building [5,9,4,1,2,3,4]. In Example 2 the shared subsequence [6,8,1] appears at positions 2, 5, 7 of arr (length 3), giving 6 − 3 = 3. The classic LCS DP fills an n×m table — up to 10^10 cells for lengths of 10^5 — which is hopeless. The saving grace is that target consists of distinct integers: relabel each value by its index in target and keep only arr entries that exist in target; a common subsequence then corresponds exactly to a strictly increasing run of ranks, so the task becomes longest increasing subsequence (LIS), solvable in O(m log m) with patience sorting.
k: Insertions only ⇒ answer = len(target) − LCS(target, arr); nothing already matching in relative order needs re-inserting.
Distinct target values let us replace every value by its position in target; LCS then equals LIS of the mapped array, because common subsequences must pick strictly increasing target indices.
Elements of arr that never appear in target are dead weight — drop them before running LIS.

a.n: Approach 1: Dynamic Programming on Longest Common Subsequence
a.i: The textbook LCS recurrence computes, for every prefix pair, the best length achievable. It directly expresses the problem's structure and is worth writing to establish the answer formula, but with both arrays up to $10^5$ long it requires ~10^10 operations and a giant table — far beyond limits.
s: Define dp[i][j] = LCS length of target[:i] and arr[:j].
Otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either side: max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).
a.t: O(n · m) — up to 10^10 cell updates at full constraints; shown for understanding only
a.sp: O(n · m) — the DP table (reducible to O(m) with rolling rows)

a.n: Approach 2: Coordinate Mapping plus LIS (Patience Sorting)
a.i: Because target has distinct values, map each value to its index. Replacing surviving arr elements by these indices turns any common subsequence into an increasing sequence of indices — and vice versa. The LIS of that mapped sequence can be computed greedily: maintain tails, where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1, updated by binary search. The final answer subtracts the LIS length from len(target).
s: Build rank[v] = index of v in target.
Convert arr into seq: for each element present in target, append its rank; skip everything else.
For each x in seq, binary-search the leftmost tail >= x (bisect_left / lower_bound): extend tails when at the end, otherwise overwrite that slot.
a.t: O(n + m log n) — building the rank map is linear; each kept arr element triggers one binary search into tails
a.sp: O(n) — the rank map and the tails buffer

w: State the reduction chain explicitly — "insertions only means answer = |target| minus LCS; distinct target values means LCS becomes LIS" — that narrative is what the interview is testing. Pitfalls: using bisect_right/upper_bound instead of bisect_left/lower_bound (target indices are distinct, so the increasing subsequence must be STRICTLY increasing); forgetting to filter arr down to values present in target; and off-by-one errors when mapping ranks. Edge cases: no overlap at all (answer is len(target)), arr already containing target in order (answer 0), and heavy duplicates in arr (harmless — duplicates just compete within the same rank). Follow-ups: allow substitutions too (edit-distance flavor), reconstruct which positions to insert, or handle duplicate values inside target where true LCS machinery would be required.
